newsitem.title: JAPAN: Corporate Japan finds cutting racketeer ties tough.
newsitem.headline: Corporate Japan finds cutting racketeer ties tough.

text.p: A fresh case of suspected payoffs to "sokaiya" racketeers on Tuesday shows yet again how tough it appears to be for corporate Japan to cut the ties that bind it to the underworld.
Foodstuff and seasonings maker Ajinomoto Co said on Tuesday that two of its senior officials had been arrested on suspicion of paying several million yen in company funds to sokaiya.
The new scandal follows revelations last week of suspected illegal dealings and possible payoffs to a one-time racketeer by Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

"Sokaiya are in a way a reflection of the underdevelopment of Japan's capitalist economy," said a Japanese executive. "It's an old practice and legal changes were supposed to halt it, but it's tough for companies to give up the old ways."

Sokaiya, often linked to "yakuza" crime syndicates, typically try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices or to make a disturbance at yearly shareholders' meetings -- called "sokai" in Japanese.
Companies have also been known to hire sokaiya to muzzle legitimate shareholders' questions at the annual meetings.

In June of last year, the president of prestigious Japanese department store Takashimaya resigned to take management responsibility for the arrest of a former executive and two officials on suspicion of payoffs to sokaiya.
Japanese law has since 1982 prohibited payoffs to sokaiya, but domestic media noted when the Takashimaya saga broke that many firms had failed to break away.
"It is clear that corporate payoffs to the racketeers have constituted a major source of underworld organisations' revenue," one newspaper lamented at the time.

The payoffs have persisted despite pleas from business groups and police for companies to stop dealings with gangsters and firms' efforts to foil the racketeers by bunching their shareholders' meetings on the same few days.

"They were having some degree of progress (in cutting ties with racketeers), but about two years ago there was an incident in which a sokaiya apparently stabbed a corporate executive in front of his house," one securities analyst said.
"That put things in a slightly different perspective."

Some experts also said sokaiya's ability to prey on management reflected a corporate stance which places little emphasis on providing legitimate shareholders with fair and equal access to information as well as indifference on the part of many shareholders to their own rights and duties.

"At most Western shareholders' meetings, shareholders ask serious questions and management tries to answer seriously," the Japanese executive said. "But in Japan, the shareholders' meeting is just a ceremony and the sokaiya are able to take advantage of that."

Japan has been hit by a plethora of corporate scandals of varied ilk in the past few years and experts say more are likely to emerge as deregulation unwinds the cosy ties that once helped to keep many misdeeds behind closed doors.
"I think we will see a lot more, and in the short term that can be painful. But in the long term, it's probably a good thing for these to come out," said one foreign executive.
